Mr. Speaker, it certainly is very depressing to hear the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) express the view that, after all, it is doubtful if anything effectual can be done, or rather if anything can be done without the co-operation of the United States, to reduce the cost of living in this country. I intend to make some reference to this phase of the question as discussed by the minister. I desire first, however, to deal with the resolution which my right hon. friend the Prime Minister has pre-
[Sir George Foster.!
sented, and to endeavour to express the reasons which I think ought to influence the House in refusing its consent to its adoption. My right hon. friend has, it is true, said, and I have no doubt said with great propriety, that he would await the declaration of the opinion of my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) as to the desirability or otherwise of passing this resolution, before he would take action upon it, either by putting it to the decision of the House or withdrawing it. The Prime Minister, as I have said, very properly stated that. Therefore in the expression of my views, I shall have no expectation that my opinions will have any very great influence, either upon that side of the House or upon this, in arriving at the decision to which my right hon. friend refers. Nevertheless, I have very strong views upon the question, and I think it desirable that I should state them to the House. My right hon. friend refers to the speeches which were made last session by himself and by the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier). He said at that time, and very truly, that there was an unanimity on the part of members on both sides of the House. He referred to the fact that during the progress of the war there had been great unanimity among the members of the House and among the people of this country. The reason for that was that there had been some respect paid to and some appreciation shown for the views of a large number of members of this House and a large section of the people of this country. The reason for that condition of affairs was that there was a manifest desire to avoid great controversial questions; questions which would divide province from province, and one section from another section, upon racial lines.
There was evidently, up to that time at all events, a desire to avoid any such action as this, and that was wise, Sir. My right hon. friend proposed that Parliament should grant to the Government an extension, because that is what it amounts to. It was not granting to this Parliament a further term of life, but it was granting to the Govetnment, which had the confidence of the majority of this Parliament, an extension of its term. My right hon. friend asked this House to grant the Government a renewal of their confidence. There did not seem to be any important questions which would divide the people. Parliament and the people of this country had a right to expect that the same policy which had been pursued previously in this war should

be continued, but the position to-day is entirely different. My right hon. friend, without any notice, without any consultation with the people of this country, and I believe without any reason to justify such a course, has thrown upon this House a measure more controversial, more calculated to array one section of the country against another, more calculated to array one class of the people of this country against other classes, and more calculated to raise racial cries in this country than any other question which could possibly have been precipitated. Yet the right hon. gentleman asks this House to give this measure its unanimous support. Notwithstanding the fact that the Government has acted contrary to the solemn pledges which the Prime Minister made to this House, and has more than once made to the people of this country, the right hon. gentleman comes forward with a coolness which, in any one else but my hon. friend, would excite surprise, and asks this House to pass a resolution renewing the confidence of this Parliament in his Government. It is astonishing that the right hon. gentleman should do that, when he knew perfectly well, before he presented the resolution, that it could not, by any possibility, be accepted by the unanimous judgment of this House. I say to my right hon. friend that, no matter what might be his views, with all his power and all the influence which he is entitled to command among the people of this country on account of the long and valued service he has given to the State, no matter how much he might endeavour to influence public opinion with his great persuasive power, I doubt if he. could convince any large number of the members sitting on this side of the House -and I am sure, Sir, that he would not be able to convince a majority, even of the people of this country-that it would be desirable to renew the confidence of this Parliament in the gentlemen who sit upon the treasury benches.
My right hon. friend says that he has been urged by many influential people to' press through this resolution as a partisan measure, and send it to the Imperial Government, and ask the Imperial Parliament to pass it. No one knows better than my right hon. friend that if he were to have this resolution adopted against the views of any large section of this country, the Imperial Government and the Imperial Parliament would refuse to carry it into effect. That is why the right hon. gentleman will not risk the passing of this resolution by a majority vote of this Parliament. They could ask a majority of the members of this House, which they command, to pass it, if they dared to do so, but they know it would be waste paper when it was passed. It might cross the ocean, but it would never find a place upon the statute books of the Imperial Parliament. My right hon. friend, in view of the pressure which has been behind him in certain quarters, makes the announcement that he will withdraw the resolution, unless it meets with the unanimous approval of this House, because he knows that it would not be carried into effect. And why? The reason was well stated by my right hon. friend, the leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laur-ier), and his words were quoted by the Prime Minister, that the Imperial Parliament would not think, for a single moment, of altering the constitution, unless they had evidence that it was with the unanimous, or practically unanimous, consent of this Parliament, which would mean the consent of both sides of the House. My hon. friend says we ought to bring our minds to a conclusion to adopt this resolution, because in times of war people ought not to pay special attention to the provisions of the constitution, and that these constitutional rights should not be regarded too solemnly.* Well, Sir, that is exactly what the Kaiser said after the war broke out. The Kaiser made up his mind that it would be of enormous advantage to get through Belgium on the triumphant march of his army to Paris. Belgium refused to let the German army pass through, and the German Government said:	"Oh, in
times of war, treaties are but scraps of paper, we will have no regard to the treaty under which we are bound to protect Belgium, because these are war times, and in war times one is justified in resorting to any measure in order to accomplish one's end.'' And so my right hon. friend says these are war times, and no regard should be had to the constitution. I regard the British North America Act as a compact between the different provinces of Canada, which cannot be broken, except by the consent of every province which became a party to that compact. That is the view which has -been taken by great public men who have addressed themselves to the question since Confederation. That is the view which has been held by the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, the highest appeal court in the Empire, and that is the view which generally prevails among constitutional lawyers. It	is	a	pact,
and cannot be broken by the voice

of three or four or five or six of the provinces of Canada, but it can only be broken by the unanimous vote of all the provinces which entered into the pact under which Confederation was formed. As I am taking a different position to-day from that which I took when I agreed to an extension of the life of Parliament at the last session, I desire tb say that one of the grounds upon which I take my stand to-day is that this Government, in utter breach of the pledge which was made to this Parliament, at a time when the Prime: Minister of Canada knew what was the view of one province of this country as to,the necessity of standing by the constitution, that there would be no compulsory service in Canada, is- attempting to force upon the country a measure of compulsory service, without the people of Canada being allowed to have any voice in it.

maintopic: EDITION
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: EDITION
speechtext:
Under these circumstances, as I indicated when speaking on the motion for second reading of the conscription Bill, I will vote against the resolution for the extension of the life of Parliament. At last session, we took an extraordinary course; but as I have said, up to that time, all was harmony; there had been no discord; there had not been thrust into the political arena any questions calculated to arouse our people either upon national or upon racial issues. But it was a step which, even for the other considerations I have mentioned, one ought to hesitate long before taking. The fact that we took that step once ought to be no precedent for our taking it again.
Why was the term of five years fixed in the constitution under which the provinces of Canada were united? Why was it not left to this Parliament to determine what should be its life? The Imperial Parliament can determine its period of life; the New Zealand Parliament and the Parliament of Australia can do the same thing; but for good and substantial reasons, for reasons which at the time seemed to be sound, the Fathers of Confederation placed in the constitution the provision that it should be beyond the power of this Parliament to extend its life. The circumstances in this country are peculiar. We have two races of equal prominence and with equal rights, two races which stand equal before the law. It could not be foreseen what might be the action of Parliament in reference to questions in which either race might be particularly concerned, and the

Fathers of lOonfederaion therefore determined that there should be a limit to the life of Parliament, and that from time to time at periods not longer than five years apart, Parliament should be dissolved and Government and Opposition should be obliged again to appeal to the people That safeguard was put into the constitution, and it should not lightly be interfered with. My right bon. friend said that it would be objectionable to have an election because it might be impossible to -take the votes of the soldiers at the front. Not many sessions ago a Bill for taking the -soldiers' votes was under consideration d-ay after day, and when -hon. members on this side dpubted the possibility of taking their votes, hon. gentlemen on the Treasury -benches replied th-at it would be the easiest thing in the world to do, and one prominent member of the Government declared publicly at that time that the whole country was crying in thunderous tones for an election -and that the soldiers' votes must be taken. The Soldiers Voting A-ct w-as therefore passed to make ample provision to that end. Yet when hon. -gentlemen opposite do not want an election; when they are afraid to submit their record to the people; w-hen there is -this issue, unclouded by any other issue, when 'they think they can raise questions which will enable them to speak eloquently of the sacrifices of our brave boy-s at the front; when they think they will be -able to sway the multitude by waving the Old Flag and thus making the people forget their wrong-doings during the past six years during which they have held the reins of office in this country-they introduced this compulsory measure, and at the same time they ask us to extend -their parliamentary lives. They are doing this -as a -means of escape from the wrath of the people in case the extension should be refused, as they knew when they introduced this resolution that it was not unlikely to be refused. We were elected fpr five years. It i-s now pretty nearly s-ix years since the people sent us here as their representatives. Many seats are unfilled; thousands of people in this country have never had -an opportunity of voting for members of this Parliament, and they -are entitled to representation. My right hon. friend, in connection with the taking of the soldiers' votes said: Many of our -brave boys at the front will not have an opportunity of voting if a general election is brought on. Of the 300,000 men who h-ave been sent -across the seas, how many have ever had had an opportunity of voting for the present members of this Parliament? The last census was taken in

1911, six years ago. Of the hoys who are now from 20 to 25 years of age and who are at the front not one has had an opportunity of voting for members of this Parliament. They were boys of from 14 to 19 when the census was taken and when the lists of 1911 were prepared. They are like thousands of other young men in this country of similar age who have never been permitted to exercise the franchise. They are entitled to exercise it. This Parliament does not represent them.
Let me present the matter in another way. What right have we, of our oWn motion and by our own votes, to extend our term of office? Hon. gentlemen on the other side who think they are little political gods, who think that they and they alone are capable of managing the affairs of the country, who think that they and they alone have a proper conception of the duty of a government in these war times, say it is for the best interest of the country that they should continue in office. That is exactly what the late ruler of Russia thought. He thought he could rule Russia much better than the people could rule. He thought he- knew much better than the people of Russia what was in their best interest. But Romanoff is now doing garden work inside the walls of a prison in southern Russia, endeavouring to increase the production of that country. His fate, however, does not dampen the ardour of hon. gentlemen opposite, nor does the fate of other autocrats who have endeavoured, without a constitution, to rule the people. I can imagine no greater evidence of a desire to continue a state of autocracy in this country than that this Government and this Parliament should Tefuse to consult the people. Hon. gentlemen opposite say: Oh, the people do not know nearly so well as we what is in their best interest; it is in their best interest that we should manage the war for them without consulting them; we set ourselves up above the people, and, therefore, because we think we can manage far better than they, it is desirable that the life of a Parliament should be extended for another year. If it is extended for another year, why not extend it still for another year? Does this Government give us any assurance that the war will end in one year from now? When the war broke out they thought and by their do-nothing policy they acted as though they thought, the war would be over in a few months. But they can give us no assurance now that the war will be over in a year. We all pray that it may be, but if it continues for still
another year, will they again ask for an extension? And if the war continues for two years, will they come again and ask for a still further extension? If they are the only people capable of governing this country, why not? If they are the only people who know how the war should be carried on, why should not they come again, and again, and again, although ten years may have passed away since the people have had an opportunity of casting their ballots?
For these reasons, I do not hesitate to say that I, for one, shall find it impossible to vote for this resolution, if I am to do justice to my conscience and perform what I believe to be my duty to the people. While I have not been over many parts of Canada,
I have had an opportunity of meeting quite a large number of people of my own province, and I have not met one single man who thinks it desirable or proper that the life of this Parliament should be further extended. That remark applies to Liberals and Conservatives alike. They say: "Let us have an election; the people ought to rule in this country; you gentlemen at Ottawa are only the servants of the people, who have chosen you for five years, and no longer, to do our work. This is our country, not yours; the interests at stake in this great war are ours, and not yours alone, except as you are part of the people. We have given you a mandate for five years, at the end of which time you are to come back to us and render an account of your stewardship, allowing hs to decide who shall represent us in Parliament for another term of five years." Does not that strike you, Sir, as a reasonable proposition in this democratic country? I think it should appeal to you and to every man in this country who has the faintest idea that it is the right of the people to rule.
I should like to address a few remarks to the amendment moved by my hon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham). If this amendment should be accepted by the Government and effect be given to it, I think it would be very much in the interests of Canada, and would do a great deal towards winning the war. I therefore hope the amendment will be carried. My hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster), in view of the magnificent things which he says and of the few things which he does, is entitled to be regarded as the most eloquent dreamer that we have in this whole Dominion. He says that this resolution is general in its character.

maintopic: EDITION
speechtext:
It was the
remarks of my hon. friend, and not the resolution, that I characterized as general.

maintopic: EDITION
speechtext: I am glad that my hon. friend, when he came to consider the amendment, saw that it was in concrete form and not so general in its character.

maintopic: EDITION
speechtext: I have not passed any opinion on that.

maintopic: EDITION
speechtext:
My hon. friend was to keep clear of that. Let me read the amendment, which strikes me as being a mighty good one to propose at this time, and one which will commend itself to the people of this country:
That all tihe words after the word "that" in the said resolution be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
In the opinion of this House the consideration of the terms of the said resolution should be deferred until the Government brings before Parliament measures providing that those best able to pay will be asked to contribute their full share to the cost of the war and by which all agricultural, industrial, transportation and natural resources of Canada will be organized so as to ensure the greatest possible assistance to the Empire in the war and to reduce the cost of living to the Canadian people.
I am particularly glad to be able to support this amendment. It seems to me to be particularly in the interests of the Canadian people. I am glad to support it because it breathes the spirit which ran throughout all the speeches which were delivered by hon. gentlemen on this side of the House in favour of compulsory military service. They, with hardly an exception, while supporting the Bill for conscripting the man-power of this country, took the ground that there were other things beside the man-power of Canada to be sacrificed; that there should be a mobilization of the resources of Canada as well; that the man-power of this country should be diverted into the best channels for the production of food, for increasing transportation facilities, for the putting of fuel on the market at lower prices, and for reducing the cost of living, which has risen at an appalling rate in this country. The first part of this resolution urges that consideration of the Government's resolution be deferred. Surely no harm could come from that. As has been pointed out,* it will be some three months, or even more, before the term of Parliament will expire, and Parliament can be kept together very easily without any one suffering greater inconvenience than any man should be

willing to put up with in the interests of the country. The amendment urges that consideration of the resolution be deferred until the Government brings before Parliament measures providing:
"That those best able to pay will be asked to contribute their full share to the cost of the war and by which all agricultural, industrial, transportation and natural resources of Canada will be organized so as to ensure the greatest possible assistance to the Empire in the war and to reduce the cost of living to the Canadian people."
My hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce says: Oh, Mir. Speaker, is it not a horrible thing to ask us to do this, when we have only three months of life before us? -when we can actually see our graves yawning before us, waiting for us to fall into them, is it not horrible to ask us to undertake this great work? Why did not the Government, undertake it long ago? This war has been on isince the 4tih of August, 1914, but these gentlemen thought it was. going to be over in a very few weeks or a few months at most. They have told this House on more than one occasion that there was danger of the Empire being at war with Germany. They told us so when, they wanted us to engage in that chimerical scheme, the building of dreadnoughts by Canada. They toild us in the August session of 1914 that Germany had been preparing for this war for forty years. Well, if they had kept in touch with the British military authorities, as was their duty, they would have known that such was the case. Do they pretend that they did not know? Did they think the war would be a triumphal march to Berlin within two or three months' time? Sir, as reasonable men they ought to have known that this war was likely to last a number of years; but whether certain that it would last a number of years or not, it was their duty to prepare for whatever eventualities might occur. Ought they not to have known that as millions of people were diverted from productive life into the ranks of the consumers, food products would become scarcer and the cost of the necessities of life would be likely to rise?
And if there is any advantage in appointing a Food Controller and a Fuel Controller to-day, was there not the same need of appointing such guardians of the people's welfare shortly after the war broke out, and was that not the time to appoint them-long before prices had soared to the enormous figures they have reached, figures which have become so alarming and which are so out of all proportion to what they

should be that people in ordinary circumstances find it difficult to keep body and soul together because they are unable to meet the cost of the necessities of life.
My right horn, friend says: What could we have done in the way of transportation? Should they not have thought for a moment that Canada is capable of becoming the granary of the world, and that with proper production and proper transportation Canada could supply the allied armies with all the flour they might require? As prudent men should they not have thought- of the future, and should they not have taken steps to endeavour to increase production, provide more transportation, and decrease its cost as far as possible? But, they have done nothing.
During last season the farmers in the West had the greatest difficulty in getting the cars necessary to, transport their products to- the markets of the world. My right hon. friend says:	"Are we to take
charge of the railways and operate them?" Not at all. Hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House are now fond of referring to what has been done in the United States -although it was not always so with them. What was done in the United States immediately after the war broke out? Within a -few days the Government wired to the ninety-one, presidents, of the railway companies in that great country, asking them to meet at Washington in order to confer upon the steps that should be taken to make the railways of the country as efficient as possible. On the day appointed 86 out of the 91 presidents- attended. The representative of the United States Government said: "Now, gentlemen, we want you to put all the railways in this country under one control. We want to operate all the railways of the United States just as if it were one great system, and if cars of one road are not particularly needed, but are required on another, these cars may be transferred at a moment's notice, irrespective of the wishes of the particular railroad. The 86 railroad presidents said: "We will gladly meet your views." By six o'clock that evening an agreement had been drawn up and signed, embodying the wishes of the Government, and since that time the railroad systems of the United States have been operated as if they were controlled by one company. An executive board was chosen consisting of five of the ablest railway men in the Upited States. They have their offices in Washington, and everything is directed by them. In this country there has been a shortage of cars or a shortage
of locomotives on one railroad, and a surplus on another, but there is jealousy between the companies here, and there is no disposition amongst them to assist one another. The Government has no control over them, and no agreement with them. I think the example of the United States in this particular instance might very well be followed. Perhaps I should not say followed, although it may not be too late to follow it. In any event, that is the course which ought to have been -adopted by this Government at the beginning. If this had been done the Government would know what rolling stock was available, and the railways should have been induced by persuasion or by assistance to piocure -all the equipment necessary to meet the transportation demands of the country. It would not have been costly to the Government, because this rolling stock could have been placed with the companies under the trust system, by which the Government would have been properly secured.
My right hon. friend says, "Think of the great number of ships which would be required to transport food to the Allies." Is not that the very reason why we should have done our part? Surely the more ships required, more obligatory would it be upon the Government of Canada to do their share of the work necessary to facilitate and cheapen transportation across the ocean. However, the Government has not done anything. Hon. members on this side of the House have pleaded in cur humble way. We have pleaded especially with the Minister of Trade and Commerce to engage in building ships in Canada, as a government undertaking. Unfortunately our appeals fell upon absolutely deaf ears. One would not have "known that the Minister of Trade and Commerce was born in a maritime section of the country. One would not have known from his inaction

I will not say his action-that he was familiar with shipbuilding. One would not have supposed for a moment that he came from a country where twenty-five, or thirty, or forty years ago there were not only hundreds, but thousands, of wooden ships constructed, which were the pridi -of that portion of Canada, and which sailed upon every sea, carrying commerce between Canada and all the countries of the world. Yet in the city of St. John, even since he and I. were boys together at college, I have seen 1,200 ablebodied men working in one shipyard. There are scores, hundreds-nay, I am almost safe in saying, thousands-of places in the Maritime Provinces which could easily be turned

into yards for the building of -wooden vessels. The hon. minister says: We could not do anything, so many were required. Is that an answer to make at this late date? Consider the way in which our people are suffering from the high cost of fuel. Take the cities in the Maritime Provinces facing upon the ocean, in open water communication with the great anthracite mines of Pennsylvania. It costs far more to bring the coal by water from the mines to those cities than it costs t'o buy coal at the point of production. This is simply because vessels are so scarce.
We have pleaded with my right hon. friend to engage in tire building of ships even for the coastal trade of Canada, even to save onr people from being frozen to death in the winter, or from 'being reduced to a state of poverty by the high price of fuel. Coal can he bought at the mines for $6 a ton, yet it has cost our people between $15 and $16 a ton. Notwithstanding this, the Government feels that no duty rests upon it to engage in the building of ships, either for the coastal service of Canada or for service across the Atlantic.
Take the cost of the other necessities of life. I will not refeT to the cost of goods kept in cold stores, because quite recently we have had a very strong report upon that subject. Take the cost of flour, for instance. My right hon. friend says, in effect: We could not control the cost of flour because some people must produce what other people eat; therefore, as somebody must produce the wheat, somebody must grind it into flour and take $15 a barrel for it, because it must be raised and milled. He promises what he is going to do when the war is over; he is going to b^iild ships. After the war is over, he is going to have a great programme for shipbuilding, but during the war the task is too mighty for him or his Government to undertake.
-Take the case of flour. It is beyond all reason, it is a disgrace to this Government that it has been allowed to jump from dollar to dollar, to jump by leaps and bounds, until it has reached a cost beyond the means of the people to pay. There was no need of it if this Government at the start had taken the proper steps-I do not mean by compulsion-but had taken steps to supervise production. If the farmers and those great associations of grain growers had been seen, a harmonious arrangement, to which they would have been glad to agree, could have been made by which the price of wheat would have been fixed at a reasonable sum. Then the

Government should have seen the mill-owners, and they should have arranged that the cost of milling would have been so much. The millers are patriotic if you approach them in the right way. They would have made a proper arrangement. If they had known that you were to approach them altogether, they would have agreed to such an arrangement-so much for the wholesale dealer in flour, so much for the retailer, so much for the baker, and all along the line from the point of production upon the farm until the flour reached the house of the consumer. In this way you could have made an arrangement which could have materially reduced the cost of living. That is the process that is being undertaken by the very eminent controller of food in the United States, Mr. Hoover. He feels that by that system he can enlist the sympathy and support of the whole people, and that the cost of production can be kept down.
The amendment speaks of organizing the industrial resources of this country. Why should that not be done? It should have been done long, long ago. Why, Sir, we have in this country great Government workshops, situated at Transcona, near Winnipeg, at a point near Quebec, and at Moncton. These could have been enlarged to such proportions as might be necessary; they have the most improved machinery, and in these shops the manufacture of munitions for the Empire could have been undertaken and carried on as a national work, paying the men a reasonable wage for their work, and allowing no profits such as have been allowed to the manufacturers of munitions under the arrangement which has been made.
Is any country in the world doing that to-day?

I do not care whether there is any country in the world doing it or not. In other countries the influence of the profiteers may be as great as it is in Canada but there is no reason why it should not be done. I will tell you why it is not done in Canada. The Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) says: Let us make this war pay for itself. He does not do it, oi course, because he is putting the burden upon posterity, but he says: Let us make the war pay for itself. He says to the manufacturers of flour: "If you can get $15 a barrel for your flour, take it. Then you have to render to me an account of yojir profits. I will let you have twenty, forty-five or fifty per cent and I will take the

balance and put it into tbe treasury? Then, I will boast to the people the enormous revenues that we are getting from the business interests of this country." What does it mean to the Minister of Finance if the Lake of the Woods Milling Company makes $1,200,000 or $2,500,000 excess profits? The larger the excess profits, the greater the revenue to the country, the more satisfactory is the Budget that he brings down and the louder will be the cheers from hon. gentlemen opposite. If there were no excessive profits, there would not be this large business tax, and there would not be this vainglory on the part of the Minister of Finance who is making this increase in his revenue out of the misery and the want of the common people of this country.
. Mr. LALOR: Where does that want or misery exist?

That want and misery is all over this country-not with the canners -no-but with the common people. That is where it exists. My hon. friend has to do nothing more than go into the homes of the people of Canada, to go to the mothers, the wives and sisters often of the soldiers who have gone to the front, to visit families who are receiving an allowance, to find want and complaints as to the high cost of living which exists among the ordinary, common people.
With regard to the industrial resources, why should not the Government in a reasonable manner have taken control of the industries which are more especially engaged in making goods for the nation? Why should they not do it now? It was not the policy of this Government that they should do it. You will remember that only a year ago, on information which I had received, I made the statement in this House that under the contracts which had been given by the old Shell Committee, the baby of the then Minister of Militia, upwards of $80,000,000 of the money of the people of the Empire and of Canada had been uselessly spent and that that large amount might have been saved if economical, prudent and businesslike methods had been pursued. I made that charge standing in my place in this House and I risked my seat in Parliament upon my ability to prove what I had stated. Hon. gentlemen on the other side, led by hon. gentlemen sitting on the treasury benches, laughed me down or tried to do it. They said: We will have none of that, why, thlat is not a crime; that is only want of judgment; that is only waste of public money; you fellows upon the other side
are charging us with extravagance and waste; why should we bother about that; $80,000,000; what is that; unless you charge that somebody stole it, we will not investigate the matter because we do not think it worthy of being investigated. I referred to a gentleman in Hamilton who had received such enormous profits that he actually became surfeited with them and became ashamed to continue making them. He offered his munition plant to the Government when Mr. Thomas was here from England. The Government did not accept his offer and they ridiculed the idea of his making these enormous profits. But later on when the same gentleman sent to the Government his cheque for upwards of $700,000, representing the enormous profits that his conscience would not permit him to keep, they took off their bats to Mr. Bailey and said: This is a great patriot and his conduct is deserving to be followed by a great many of the other munition manufacturers in this country.
So far as I have seen in the public press, that example has not been followed by others. I have just a few words to say after recess, and perhaps we had better call it six o'clock.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess.
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

maintopic: EXTENSION OF THE TERM OF PARLIAMENT.

speechtext: The order for Private Bills having been exhausted, the House resumed consideration of the proposed resolution of Sir Robert Borden (Prime Minister) for the extension of the paliamentary term, and the amendment thereto proposed by Mr. Graham.

maintopic: EXTENSION OF THE TERM OF PARLIAMENT.
speechtext:
Before recess, I was endeavouring
to reply to a statement by my right hon. friend, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) that this Government could not do anything more than it had done. It seems to me that, so far as shipping is concerned, the Government has utterly failed to discharge its duty to the people of Canada and to the Allies. It has been stated on several occa-



sions by members of the Government that, because the Imperial Munitions Board are building some ships an Canada, the Government is relieved of any obligation in that direction. I take >a view entirely contrary to that. A great many people think that this Government is building ships, and are disposed to give it some credit for this action; but the Government are doing nothing of the kind. They absolutely declined to do anything, though they -were urged over and over again by members pn this side of the House to engage in this moat important work. The work has been, to a limited extent, taken up by the Imperial Munitions Board, who have laid down the standard, and are having some vessels, m.ostly wooden vessels, built in Canada. But they are by no means exhausting the facilities which exist in Canada, or the men who are available. I have the knowledge, Sir, that quite recently different people have communicated with a shipbuilding director of the Munitions Board offering to build ships, asking for contracts, and they have been told that the board are not in a position to give any more contracts at the present time, and that they have no authority to give contracts, and only to-day I met some gentlemen from the Pacific coast, who informed me that the same statement was made to them by the Imperial Munitions Board. That corroborates the statement which was made to gentlemen in the Maritime Prov-incese who are very desirous of engaging in the work. If this Government, even at this late day, were to offer contracts for the building of wooden vessels, to be owned by the Government-so that the freight rates could be kept down within reasonable limits, which would perform enormous service to the country-I have no doubt they could find plenty of people, both on the Atlantic and the Pacific coasts, on the St. Lawrence river and on the Great Lakes, who would be willing to engage in the work, and who would gladly accept contracts from the Government. Therefore, when the Government, through its Minister of Trade and Commerce, says that it can do nothing in the way of shipbuilding, it is confessing its own inability to carry on in an ordinary businesslike way the affairs of this country.
With regard to the farming interests, the minister says: Oh, see what we have done for the farmers. They have done only what they were doing in peace times; they have not changed in any way from what they were doing before the war broke out. They have been following largely along the line 
laid down by* their predecessors. It is true they have been giving encouragement to agriculture, but that is all. There has been no organization of labour, no special encouragement given to the farmer, nothing more done for the encouragement of agriculture than 'has been done in peace times, when there was not the same demand for food.
The .minister iasks: Wlhat can be done? T!he question is, what has this Government not done for the farmer? What they have not done would fill volumes, and what .they have done would fill only a page ot two. In the matter of fertilizers, other countries aro giving great encouragement. We know whait (Germany and Australia have dope. 'So far from doing anything to encourage farmers to get cheap fertilizers and abundance of them, this Government has actually imposed a tax upon fertilizer, taxing the most essential raw material of the farmer. Is that giving proper encouragement? Is that stimulating food production? Then, any one who has given any attention to agriculture to-day knows there is nothing of greater importance, as fax as food production is concerned, than the extensive use of tractors. I do not mean the large tractors used by wealthy people, but the smaller tractors which can be bought at a reasonable price, a price which the ordinary farmer will be able to .pay. But when a farmer attempts to obtain one of these tractors, he finds he is met with a duty of from 25 to 30 .per cent. I am within the knowledge-and I am sure within the judgment-of my horn, friends who come from the West when I say that a reasonable encouragement 'by taking the duty off these tractors would enormously stimulate the production of grain in our western country. The Government have not responded to the demand made by the farmers. Not long ago the )hon. member from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) introduced a resolution in the House urging that the duty upon farm implements, including tractors, should be removed. That resolution met with a determined opposition from the Government and its followers, and it was voted down by the Government majority in this House. Is that the way to encourage the farmer? Yet that is what this Government has done. They have imposed this heavy burden for the protection of one or two large manufacturers who are making these large tractors in Canada, preventing the farmer from getting them iu from the United States on the easiest terms possible. To-day we have in every

province in Canada 'hundreds and thousands of men who are not familiar with horses, men living in the cities, towns and villages, who would be glad to get on the farms and be glad to operate these tractors, in order to do this essential work of farm production. Yet the Government give no encouragement whatever in this direction.
Then, with regard to the development of the West, if the Government, early in this war, had placed wheat and wheat products, and oats and cattle upon the free list-particularly wheat and wheat products, which would' have ensured a free entry for those products info the markets of the United States-it would have had the effect of encouraging the farmers to engage more vigorously and enthusiastically in farming upon a larger scale, because they would have had assurance that, even if the English and Canadian markets were to fall off, there would still 'be a market in the United States, and when prices went down there would be a demand which would always ensure a fair return for their products. It would have had an enormous effect, and yet because these gentlemen are tied to the principle of a high protective tariff they refused, and have refused over and over again, the offers which have been made on behalf of the people of the West by members upon this side of the House, and they have voted down resolutions urging that encouragement in this direction should be given to agriculture.
With regard to men, what have they done? Have they endeavoured in any way to organize the man power of this country for the purpose of assisting in agriculture? Not at all. They make admirable speeches upon the subject; they make appeals to the farmers to produce all they can; but, so far as organization is concerned, they have utterly failed to do anything. How easy it would be to look over this country and find out where farm labour could be secured, and have that farm labour distributed where it is most needed. That is a way in which something might be done to organize the agricultural forces of the country. Only to-day I saw in the newspapers that the Prime Minister, having been waited upon by farmers from Ontario, made an appeal to the young men of the cities to go on to the farms and assist the farmers. But, so far as organization or effective work is concerned, the Government have failed to do anything.
Having made these remarks with regard to the amendment, which, as I have said, commends itself to me as one member of
221i
this House, and which I shall be glad to support, I should like to revert to the resolution itself. My right hon. friend has put forward, as a reason why we should extend the political lives of the members of this Parliament and the life of the Government, that an election at the present time Would be very objectionable because it would distract the people's attention from work in connection with the war. If this Military Service Bill goes into effect, there will he no need of any voluntary effort on the part of the people. The mandate of the Government has gone forth virtually stopping voluntary enlistment in this country. Unfortunately they will not want the people at large to pay any special attention to voluntary enlistment, because the young men of the country, if this measure goes into effect, are to be compelled by force of law to enlist in the army. The services of the Government will not be required very much in connection with the working out of the Military Service Bill, because there are provided throughout the country tribunals which will determine questions of exemption. The Government have created a Hospitals Commission; they have created a Returned Soldiers' Commission; they have Sir George Perley as overseas Minister of Militia; they have commissions for everything which can be conceived of under the sun to attend to all matters to which a Government would ordinarily he supposed to attend. Therefore, I do not see any great reason why the services of some of the ministers at all events might not be given for the purpose of enlightening the people of the country in case a general election should come on.
A suggestion has been made that a general election will divide the people. Can the people be more divided than they have been by the compulsory measure which has been brought down in this Parliament by the Prime Minister? A general election, as compared with the enforcement of the-Military Service Bill by a moribund Parliament 'with no mandate of the people- legislation which a large section of the population, of this country believe this Parliament has no right to- enact-would be, in comparison with the present condition,, like a Sunday school picnic as compared; with a circus. I do not fear any disastrous results from a general election. Why should there be? The people of this country know their rights; they know it is their right to go to the polls and deposit their ballots silently for the candidates of their choice.

They will, under ordinary circumstances, do that quietly as good citizens, and therefore I see no reason in the world to fear any great disturbance amongst the people in case of an appeal being made to them. A general election is the only safe course to pursue. A majority in this House, in the exercise of its judgment, has determined that the question of compulsory service shall not be left to the people to decide by means of a referendum. Some of us think a referendum: would have been the 'better course to pursue, because, after all, if you want to havie a peaceful, well-satisfied and contented people, you must let them realize that they are the rulers of the country, and that their voice is to prevail, Had this question been left to the people by means of a referendum, the most beneficial results would have been brought about; but as a large majority of this House has thought otherwise, the only solution of the important questions which have arisen is to submit those questions to the people at a general election.
The view that I am compelled to take is that this _Govemment must in the national interest dissolve Parliament and go to the country. To take any other course w-ould be disastrous to the future of Canada. I do not see why, when an election comes on, it -should be necessary to incite the people to any action which might be regretted. I do not -see why all the people should not go to the polls quietly and prayerfully, in view of the great crisis which confronts this country as a part of the Empire, and exercise their right with a just regard for the welfare of Canada. They 'have a great and splemn duty to perform, and I believe they will perform it prayerfully and -in the best interest of Canada and of the Empire. I feel most sincerely and deeply that if this Government attempts to bring into force this compulsory measure, to which a vast section of our pe.ople is bitterly opposed, it will lead not merely to national trouble, but to national disaster. It is unfortunate that that should he the case; but it is the case; and are we, as members of this Parliament, who, although we are living beyond our term perhaps have the right to speak for the people, to leave it an the power of these gentlemen to plunge this country into that dreadful condition which for generations would be deplored? The only hope of the country is that -these gentlemen shall face their master and ours; that they shall go -before the people in -order that the people m-ay have an opportunity of saying who shall.govem this coun-

try in -the future. These gentlemen know that while they are temporarily in command of the ship of State, they are driving to-wards the breakers. They are like drunken sailors in charge of a ship who are wilfully running their ship on the wrong course and directing it towards the breakers. It is -the right of the people-and I as one member' of this House, purpose doing my part towards allowing the people to exercise their right-to remove these gentlemen from the ship and place in charge of it men in whom the people will have confidence.

Mr. Speaker, there has been standing on the Order Paper since the 23rd of May the resolution which the right hon. leader of the Government moved this afternoon, after this long delay. For three years this country has been engaged in a great war and has called upon her citizens to contribute an enormous number of men to assist in the cause of the Allies. My hon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) presents a resolution this afternoon urging that before the House proceeds to consider the terms of the resolution introduced by the Prime Minister, the interests of the country and our position with regard to the war demand that certain steps should be taken. To that the Minister of Trade and Commerce makes an answer in which he eulogizes the services that have heon ren

dered by our men at the front, and declares in the apt and eloquent language of which he is a master, that the necessity for putting into force the Military Service Act is very great indeed which was no answer at all to the argument made by my hon. friend from South Renfrew; in fact, it was entirely irrelevant, and particularly inapropos in view of the reasons advanced by the Premier as to the imperative necessity of passing the Military Service Bill. If that Bill is of such an imperative character why has it been laid aside since last Friday? Its third reading has been absolutely postponed and its passage through this House and Parliament delayed in order that my right hon. friend might move his resolution for the extension of the parliamentary term.

maintopic: EXTENSION OF THE TERM OF PARLIAMENT.
speechtext:
It was well understood that the only reason for asking that the Bill remain in committee was that hon. members might have a reprinted copy showing what changes had been made. The Bill was printed and circulated among hon. members on Saturday, and my right hon. friend could have gone on with the Bill on that day, and it could have received its third reading; but he delayed the consideration of this imperative measure to submit this resolution which has been standing on the Order Paper since the 23rd of May. I am sure hon. gentlemen must be struck by the peculiar circumstances surrounding my right hon. friend's action. His suggestion that the delay is due to my hon. friend from Edmonton is one which will hardly be taken seriously by hon. gentlemen behind him. The House well knows that that was not the true reason why the third reading of the Military Service Bill was not proceeded with. I repeat, the Bill should have been disposed of before this resolution was introduced, and my right hon. friend should have stated to the House
what legislation he proposes to introduce before prorogation. Surely this Parliament has a right to know what action is contemplated by the Government in regard to such important legislation as the railway situation-a situation which the Minister of Trade and Commerce bad already told the House would be dealt with by a measure to be submitted to Parliament. The introduction of this particular resolution at this particular juncture, having regard to the Military Service Act, does not indicate that my right hon. friend has altogether forgotten the art of playing politics. '
What have we done in the last three years? We have given liberally of our men. The call to service made throughout this land has been responded to in a magnificent manner, and when at the end of three years of war my hon. friend from South Renfrew asks Parliament to declare that certain things are essential and must be done, can any hon. gentleman complain that his resolution is unreasonable? In his resolution he asks that those best able to pay shall contribute their full share to the cost of the war. The Minister of Trade and Commerce argued, eloquently that .there should be no contribution from these gentlemen, and then wound up by announcing that the Government proposed to bring down an income tax. Now, if an income tax is a good thing today, if it is right that the wealth of the country should contribute towards the carrying on of the war, why is it that the Government have postponed dealing with this problem until they were compelled at the point of the pistol presented by the hon. member from South Renfrew? Three months ago hon. gentlemen on this side of the House urged the Minister of Finance to deal with this question of accumulated wealth. We urged that the men of wealth who had not contributed in man-power should be made to contribute of their wealth; in other words, as my hon. friend: from South Renfrew proposes in his resolution, we urged that those best able to pay be made to contribute their full share to the cost of the war. And what did the Minister of Finance say? He said that some time, perhaps, in the future they might take up this question, but he was opposed to an income tax; it would cost too much to collect. Do you want me to tax a few wealthy men in this country, he asked, and he argued that the municipalities were already taxing the people, and this Government, therefore, should not tax them. We have been told frequently since the war began

that everybody should carry on business as usual. We have heard hon. gentlemen opposite speaking in laudatory terms of tjie Minister of Finance, telling us that he had done wonderful things in connection with financing the war and that he was in fact a paragon of financial wisdom. In the face of such a record as that, in the face of his declaration repeated over and over again in this House that he was opposed to making those best able to pay* contribute more than they were then doing, the statement of the Minister of Trade and Commerce to-night that it was the Government's intention to introduce an income tax requires a little more explanation before hon. gentlemen in this House can accept it with any degree of certainty. If it is the Government's intention to introduce a measure of this kind, why doek not my hon. friend tell us just what they propose to do?
If you follow what the Minister of Finance indicated he would do, you would have a measure so absolutely parsimonious and so absolutely incomplete that it would be a taxation measure in name only, because I assume the Minister of Finance talked by the book and laid down what he deemed to be his policy when he spoke here in May, and that we are not going to have another complete somersault upon this question and another taxation measure put in force entirely different from the one the Minister of Finance asserted never could be put on the statute. It seems to me that this proposition is one of such a serious character that before this House passes upon the matter as to whether extension should be given to this Government we should know whether or not that class of people are going to be compelled to do their share in the war, either under the Military Service Act or by the conscription of wealth. As to what will be done we have nothing to go upon but the record of the Government during the last three years, and the House and the people will not have to be told what that record means.
In regard to the question of organization referred to in the amendment, what has been the situation for three years? Absolute and complete disorganization in every matter that relates to national welfare and national interest. When the United States entered the war, there came across the ocean experts from each of the Allied countries, who consulted with the United States experts representing the Government. They laid down a programme in regard to agriculture, industry, transportation, and natural resources, which in-IMr. Macdonald.1
eludes minerals. The United States, in conference with all these gentlemen representing the Allied countries, proceeded to organize the country to render the fullest service in every one of these matters. Up to date that has not been done in Canada. My hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce told us what the Government had done in regard to the farms. Does any one seriously suggest there has been any organization, either in regard to agriculture or in regard to anything else, whereby we should render the best possible aid to the Allies? My hon. friend cannot be serious in that suggestion. Why have we not done in Canada what was done in the United States? Why did not those delegations which came across from the Allied nations visit Canada? Why was not a conference held, not merely with one gentleman down in Washington, but with all the representatives of the varied interests in Canada, so that we might be able to organize to send food and minerals to Great Britain and the Allies? But the Government stands before the country with reference to every one of those propositions absolutely without any organization, absolutely without any combination by which the full services of Canada might be rendered to the Allies.
So in regard to the question of the cost of living. The Minister of Trade and Commerce argued that you could not deal with the problem of the cost of living during the war, and with that amplitude of language which is at his command at all times, proceeded to declare the task was an impossible one. Yet there has been laid upon the table of this House and placed in the hands of the honi members a document prepared by this Government's own officials declaring that in regard to the production of bacon and ham one concern alone has been permitted to make over three million dollars of profits which they should not have been permitted to make. Still this Government sits supinely, and has sat since that report was brought down.

Graham) in the light of these facts, asks this House to declare that legislation for the purpose of providing against these conditions and for remedying these abuses should be placed upon the statute-books of this country before this Government asks for an extension of term. maintopic: EXTENSION OF THE TERM OF PARLIAMENT.
speechtext:
I wish to occupy the attention of the House for a very few minutes only. In the first place, to my mind the resolution which was introduced by the Prime Minister to-day should not have been introduced. These are times when, as we all know, there is much unrest politically, socially and otherwise, and it does appear to me that in
view of the grave question which has been before the House for some considerable time, and upon which the minds of all have been focussed, it would have been only right and propeT .and in the national interest that a motion for the extension of the life of this Parliament should have been postponed until the Bill had passed its third reading and become law of the land.
Had the motion of my hon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) declaring that the consideration of the extension of the term-of Parliament is inopportune at this time, been brought in on the third reading of this Bill, it would have been considered by the Government, and rightly so, a want of confidence motion, and it would therefore have been voted down. But let me read this amendment as it stands:
That In the opinion of this House the consideration of the terms of said resolution should be deferred.
That is all the motion asks and that is all my hon. friend asks-that it should be deferred. I claim the right to say what I propose saying in the light of my remarks upon the second reading of this Bill. May I as one who voted for conscription, for which I make no apology, say that this House and this Government should not, when declaring that they should spill the blood of men, be afraid to spill the rich man's money. That position I take tonight just as absolutely, as consistently, and as sincerely as I did on the occasion to which I have referred.
I listened to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) this afternoon. I always listen to him with interest. But, during his speech to-day, it did appear to me that he put up straw men simply to knock them down. He accused my hon. friend from South Renfrew of saying that there should be taxation of accumulated wealth and then he asked: "Would you take the mines, the minerals, the timber, the capital and all those various other things, how could you tax accumulated wealth as far as they are concerned?" In that I wholly agree with him but within the four corners of this amendment there is not one word or sentence about the taxation of accumulated wealth. The only thing that the resolution does say, and properly say, is that those who can pay shall pay. The Minister of Trade and Commerce says: "I admit the sentiments are good but they are entirely irrelevant to this motion; in my humble opinion what we need is men and more men and the men must go." Now, I absolutely and entirely agree with him but I want to ask him in

all seriousness if men and more men are to go, if men are to be drilled, equipped and sent overseas for the defence of this Empire, as they ought to be, where is the money coming from to do these necessary things? The minister says: "You will see that we have in reality conscripted wealth; look what we have done by our business tax-in 1915-16, $20,000,000 and in 1916-17 another $20,000,000!" I want to ask any hon. member within sound of my voice if he thinks that throughout the great and broad Dominion of Canada $20,000,000 a year is the sum and substance of what the rich men ought to give by way of a tax for the purpose of carrying on this war. Where is Canada and where is her wealth?
In so far as the Minister of Trade and Commerce has to-day declared on behalf of the Government that an income tax will be instituted in this country and will be brought before this House, and in view of the further fact that a food controller has been appointed by this Government, a man of ability who ought to do well, I am quite free to admit that the Government have gone some considerable way down the road towards the amelioration of conditions and the shaping of affairs as they ought to be. Provided that income tax is fair and equitable, I shall have no hesitation in supporting that particular measure.
Speaking for myself personally, as the only one for whom I can speak, I have been for a long time, and am to-day, in accord with the idea that union, or national government should have been instituted in this country. I do not believe that with the great problems that have confronted us since the war broke out, and that are facing us to-day, Canada has any right to be governed by a partisan, or party, government. The issues are large, the issues will be larger, and had it been possible, I believe we should have had, call it a union, national, or other kind, of a government, in which the very best brains of the Dominion should he united for the purpose of taking care of the affairs of this country, neither for one part nor the other, but purely in the interest of Canada and the Empire. Although I have been strongly in favour, and perhaps an advocate, of that system of government,
I believe honestly and sincerely that with the different elements on both sides of the House of Commons to-day, a national, or union government is not possible.
One reason, and not the only reason, why it is not possible is that this Parliament has now continued for six years; it has outlasted its time longer than any other Parliament in the history of Canada. Many
I .Ur. i'arde?.!
great questions have come up for consideration, and the mandate with which we were sent here in 1911 has expired. The Government have been in power for the same length of time, and their actions have not been submitted to the people for approval nor has their mandate been renewed. This Government has been in power for that length of time and has endured such a stress and strain as no other Government has endured. It has had to deal with new questions, great questions, greater than have come before any other Government in Canada. I say that the people of this country are of the opinion, whether rightly or wrongly, that there are many questions upon which they desire to pronounce. They, say that, in so far as this House is concerned, in view of the recent redistribution of seats, there are forty-three seats vacant in this House to-day; in other words one-fifth of The great Dominion of Canada is unrepresented. Taking all those things into consideration, the firm and well considered judgment of the people of Canada is, that, whether we have national or party Government, the will of the people should be asked and the will of the people should be obeyed, whatever it may be. I utter those sentiments and those opinions in absolutely no party spirit whatever.

For those reasons, Sir, I believe that the amendment moved by the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) is in the right interest, that it is in an interest that helps the boys at the front and their mothers and daughters and wives. We and they should at least know that, if the sacrifice of life is asked of them, we in this House of Commons are men enough to ask, to demand, and to insist upon the sacrifice of the rich men's money.

Mr. Speaker, I do not rise for the purpose of making a speech, but simply to make a statement in respect to the issue now before the House. I listened to the remarks of the right hon. the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) this afternoon as he presented a request to the Parliament of Canada that the term of this Parliament should be extended for twelve months. I shall read the main part of the resolution:-
1.Notwithstanding anything in the British North America Act, 1867, or in any Act amending the same, or in any Order in Council, or terms or conditions of Union, made or approved under the said Act, or under any Act of the Canadian Parliament, the term of the Twelfth Parliament of Canada is hereby extended until the seventh day of October, 1918.'
I regard that as the only question before the House this evening, and no matter what hon. gentlemen opposite may say, no matter what efforts are made to becloud the issue, this House and the people of Canada understand that this is the issue before them now for consideration and settlement. I differ with my hon. friend, and I say that the hon. member for West Lambton (Mr. Pardee) does not speak for the people of the province of Ontario when he says that the
people of Ontario are in favour of a general election in war time.
